notes.meaning: Five sisters named Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah came forward from the tribe of Manasseh. Their father Zelophehad had died without leaving any sons to receive land in Canaan. Even though Israel had not yet conquered the country, these women trusted God's promise and boldly asked for their family's share.

The sisters brought their petition right to the doorway of the sacred tent, where the nation's leaders held court. They presented their case directly to Moses, Eleazar the high priest, the tribal chiefs, and the whole assembly. Making such a public legal claim took extraordinary faith and courage for women in the ancient world.

The daughters explained that their father did not take part in Korah's famous rebellion against the Lord. If he had joined that revolt, his family might have lost their rights as traitors. Instead, he died during the long wilderness journey like the rest of his generation, leaving behind no sons.

The sisters asked why their father's family name should disappear simply because he had no sons. They requested their own piece of land among their uncles so their family line would continue. Their request showed great love for their family and deep confidence in God's promises.

Moses did not try to settle this new and difficult problem on his own. He brought their legal claim directly before the Lord to learn what was right. Good leaders show true wisdom when they seek God's direction before making important choices.

The Lord told Moses that Zelophehad's daughters were speaking the truth. God commanded that they be given a permanent inheritance among their father's brothers, passing his land rights directly to them. The Lord honoured their faith and protected the rights of families who had no sons.

God turned this specific decision into a lasting rule for all of Israel. Whenever a father died without leaving a son, his land was to pass directly to his daughter. This established an ongoing legal protection for daughters across every tribe.

The law also set out the order of inheritance if a man left no children at all. His land would go to his brothers, or next to his father's brothers, or finally to his closest living relative in the clan. This permanent ordinance kept ancestral land safely within the original tribe and family line.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars observe that this narrative illustrates how case law developed in ancient Israel, where new real-life problems were brought to God and established lasting legal precedents.

notes.meaning: The Lord told Moses to climb the Abarim mountain range to look across the river at the Promised Land. Although Moses was not allowed to cross into Canaan himself, God graciously let him view it with his own eyes. This panoramic view gave Moses a comforting sign that God would surely keep His promises.

God told Moses that after seeing the land, he would die and be gathered to his people just like his brother Aaron. In Scripture, being gathered to one's people means joining the faithful forefathers in rest rather than being lost in death. Moses could approach the end of his earthly journey in peaceful trust.

The Lord reminded Moses why he could not lead Israel into Canaan. At the waters of Meribah, Moses and Aaron had failed to uphold God's holy name before the people when they struck the rock in frustration. Even the most faithful leaders must face the earthly results of their disobedience.

Instead of complaining about his approaching death or trying to promote his own family, Moses prayed for the nation. He addressed God as the Maker who gives breath and spirit to all living people, asking Him to appoint the next leader. A godly leader cares deeply about the spiritual health of the people who come after him.

Moses asked for a leader who would guide the people in daily life and lead them in battle. He pleaded that the Lord's congregation would never be left wandering like sheep without a shepherd. This caring request points forward to Jesus Christ, the Good Shepherd who perfectly guards His flock.

The Lord directed Moses to choose Joshua, a man who already had God's Spirit guiding his life. Moses was told to place his hands on Joshua in front of the people. This act of laying on hands publicly set Joshua apart for his new task and transferred official authority to him.

Moses was commanded to have Joshua stand before Eleazar the high priest and the whole assembly. There Moses would give Joshua his formal charge and commission him for leadership. Doing this before all the people ensured that everyone recognised Joshua as God's chosen leader.

Moses was instructed to share some of his authority with Joshua right away. Working together as partners helped the people learn to respect and follow Joshua while Moses was still alive. This smooth transition protected the nation from confusion when Moses finally departed.

Joshua would lead differently than Moses did, since Moses had spoken with God face to face. Joshua was told to consult Eleazar the high priest, who would ask God for guidance using the sacred stones called the Urim. This arrangement meant that the civil leader and the priest had to work together in humble obedience to God.

Moses faithfully did everything the Lord told him to do without any envy or bitterness. He brought Joshua before Eleazar and the people, laid his hands on him, and charged him to lead the nation. Moses gladly stepped aside so that God's plans for Israel could go forward.
